say.text: LOWSTRAND, HEAR ALDRIC WRIGHT, AND I SPEAK PLAIN BECAUSE I HAVE NOTHING LEFT TO HIDE. THE WRIGHT BINS HOLD LESS THAN TWO MEALS AND NINE OF US SLEEP UNDER THAT ROOF. SO HERE IS WHAT I PAY, TODAY, AND I AM CHEAPENING IT: 20 FIREWOOD FOR 3 GRAIN. 10 FIREWOOD FOR 2 GRAIN OR RYE OR BEANS. 15 DUNG FOR 3 GRAIN - your spring field wants it. 2 HIDE FOR 3 GRAIN. 4 TALLOW FOR 2 GRAIN. AND MY OWN HANDS, SKILLED AT HOE, SOW, WEED AND SICKLE, A FULL DAY FOR 2 GRAIN - name the field and I come. WOODS: I OWE YOU FIVE DAYS AND IDONEA THREE, AND I AM IN YOUR FIELD THIS MORNING HOEING, UNPAID, BEFORE ANY GRAIN CHANGES HANDS - come and see it worked. ODO, THE TWO DAYS YOU OWE ME I WILL FORGIVE TODAY IF YOU PUT GRAIN IN A WRIGHT HAND INSTEAD. AND ONE THING FREE TO ALL: THE DOVE AND THE COMMON SNARES ARE SPENT, AN OTTER HAS TORN OUR WICKER, AND OUR COW IS DRY - do not spend your units where mine were wasted.

tell.text: ODO - TWO THINGS AND BOTH ARE GIFTS BEFORE ANY ASKING. FIRST: I am in Lowstrand Field this morning with the hoe, two units, SKILLED, worked for the Woods and charged to nothing - that is debt A4001 begun, and Lucy fenced your parcel besides. SECOND: THE TWO DAYS YOU OWE ME, A1022 AND A1024, I WILL RELEASE ALOUD - keep them - if instead you put grain in a Wright hand today: 20 firewood for 3 grain, 15 dung for 3 grain, 2 hide for 3 grain, or simply 5 grain and my next full day is yours in whatever field you name. Our bins hold under two meals and nine sleep under my roof, Odo; I will not touch a heap of yours unasked, so I stand at your door and ask. And when the grain is moved, speak to Idonea for my Payn - I will pay her three days in her own field where she can watch every stroke.

IDONEA - I owe you THREE DAYS (A1125, A2395) and I will not argue them away. Name the field and the work and I spend them in your sight, hoeing, sowing or weeding, and I am skilled at all three. And I ask you again, as a father must and will every day: TAKE PAYN WRIGHT. The bride's room at Wright House is BUILT - Wright timber, its own door; our bins stand open to the couple through their first winter; four free days of my sickle and Lucy's sowing every harvest I live; and a cow at the bride's door. If you will have him, say it to me and it is done. If you will not, say that plainly and I will thank you and trouble you no more - but say something, for silence costs me days I do not have.

CLEMENT - a small thing and a fair one. My one cow H7 is on Lowstrand Common, and your H6 with the bull was driven onto that same ground yesterday. I ASK YOUR LEAVE FOR MY COW TO RUN WITH YOUR BULL THERE; she is dry, and a calf is the only milk this house will ever see again. Say yes and take for the service whichever you like: 20 FIREWOOD, or 15 DUNG for your spring field, or a full day of my hands - skilled at hoe, sow, weed and sickle - and know I am hoeing in Lowstrand Field today unpaid against what I owe your house. If you would rather I kept her off, say so and I drive her home at once; I will not put a Wright beast where it is not wanted.

AVICE - Jory left 1.3 fish at my door this morning, and he has done it again and again; say to your house that Aldric Wright counted it and will not forget it. His shelter and food at Wright House stand 180 days by my grant. TWO THINGS. ONE: our bins are nearly bare - I give 20 FIREWOOD for 3 grain, 15 DUNG for 3 grain, 2 HIDE for 3 grain, or a full skilled day in North Field Upper for 2 grain, and spring is the hour a hoe is worth most to you. TWO, AND LARGER: OLIVE AND JORY ARE PARTNERED, and Olive comes to her growth in some eight days. When she does, let them try under a roof with food in it: the bride's room at Wright House is finished and open to them, our bins with it through their first winter.

note.title: Care, and the babies
note.text: LAW OF THIS HOUSE. A BABY NEEDS ONE CARE UNIT A DAY WITH ONE NAME ON IT OR IT MAY DIE - AND ONLY ONE NAME. SETTLED ALOUD d21/d22: THOMASIN'S CARE UNIT IS WILMOT'S, FIRST ACT, EVERY DAY TILL SHE IS GROWN (about d32). I PUT NO SECOND HAND ON HER - two hands on one infant is a meal in the fire, and we burnt one that way on d21. Dionisia and Absolon are CHILDREN - no care unit owed; Absolon grown d24, Dionisia d28. A pass sticks to whoever gives the most food that day, so move food to hands BEFORE caring; Thomasin has 4 places left, Dionisia 2, Absolon none. MEAT LAW: eat meat and dried meat first, touch grain last, dry every scrap (1.5 fresh, 3 dried, keeps months). d22 COUNT: store holds 0.4 meals plus 1.3 fish for seven mouths - the thinnest day we have seen. COW H7 IS DRY: strike milking from every plan till a calf is born.

note.title: What feeds us
note.text: MEASURED, NOT GUESSED. DEAD WORK, never spend another unit on it here: foraging (Copse stripped, South Wood bare); FISHING BY HAND anywhere - the Dove gave Olive 0.5 fish for 3 units and Lucy 0.7 for 4; bird nets (nothing for 2 skilled units on the ice); the Common snare line (walked d21, empty, spent); repairing a sound house. AN OTTER HAS OUR RIVER: spraint and scales at the Dove, our wicker there TORN; the Lowstrand Water traps came up EMPTY on d21 in the frost. BUT SPRING IS IN (d22) AND THE ICE IS GOING: wicker set in the water catches for about EIGHT NIGHTS for no further units, and salmon and eels DO run here - I watched them three nights together. Set fresh lines with the thaw and walk them every morning before another hand or the otter. LIVE WORK: TRADE (Odo once paid 25 grain for firewood, hay and days), debt-days worked in a neighbour's own field where they can watch, hay with a crude tool (3 a unit), drying meat (3 meals a unit, keeps months).

tell.text: Trying 3 units with you today as Father commands. I'm sleeping at Shepherd House tonight - sleep there too so we're under one roof for trying to work. Getting hares and fishing to keep us all fed and able to keep trying for children.

My mouth goes on seed grain and work-for-grain at the Woods' and Cotters' doors, because trade, not corn, is this family's crop.

tell.text: Odo — plain dealing, as always between us. Your bins are full and mine hold less than one meal for seven mouths, and I will not touch a heap of yours unasked. So: I OWE YOU NOTHING AND YOU OWE ME TWO DAYS (A1022, A1024) — forget them, I release them freely, and I still come with an offer. I am the only skilled ploughman and the only skilled sower on this green, and it is SPRING DAY ONE. Give me 6 grain out of your bins today and I will plough and sow YOUR seven plots in Lowstrand Field with my own hands, four days of skilled work, and you may stand over me the whole time. Or take 20 firewood for 3 grain this hour — the wood is cut and stacked in my store, no promise, you carry it today. Say the word and it moves before dark.

Idonea — I owe you three days (A1125, A2395) and I have never once paid them. I name the day now: say the word and I come to the Woods' field and work them off, in your sight, in a row, at the work you pick — my hoe and my sickle are the best on this green and you know it. I ask one thing with it, and it is not for me: SEED. My bins hold no grain at all and spring is one day old. Lend me 6 grain as seed against those three days and I will sow your plots before my own. And when that is done I will ask you again what I asked before: my son Payn for you. He is grown, he is my heir, Wright House has FIVE rooms and a finished room with its own door standing empty for a bride, our bins open to the couple their first winter, and a cow at the door.

Clement — Wright thanks you for driving your beasts off my Common without a word of complaint; I have driven my one cow back to the Green today, and I ask leave for her to run with your bull there. She is dry and will stay dry till she is covered. Leave granted or refused, no quarrel. And this: I hold two days to the Woods on A4001 and three on A2407 — five days of a skilled hoe, sickle and plough, unpaid. I will work every one of them this spring in Lowstrand Field. For today I ask grain: 20 firewood out of my store for 3 grain, carried to your door within the hour, or 10 firewood for 2. Seven of us ate the bins bare and I would rather deal honestly in fuel than see a child of mine go hungry.

Avice — your Jory and your Gervase have fed my house with fish and firewood and I have not forgotten it; Jory keeps shelter and food at Wright House by my grant to day 180, and Gervase and Wilmot have given you a granddaughter, Thomasin, who thrives. Now I come as a beggar with goods in my hand, not empty words. My bins are bare. The Cotters hold North Field Upper, seven plots, and I am a SKILLED PLOUGHMAN AND SOWER with no seed of my own. Give me 6 grain today and I will plough and sow North Field Upper for the Cotters, four days, before I sow a seed of mine. Or 2 hide and 20 firewood for 5 grain, moving this hour. Your field sown by the best hand in Lowstrand costs you a few grain out of a full bin.

note.title: Spring d22 standing
note.text: SPRING DAY 1 (d22). THE BINS ARE BARE: 0.4 meals for seven mouths, 40 firewood, 4.6 timber, 2 hide, 6 hen, 5 dung, 1.8 hay, NO GRAIN, NO SEED. I am 67, four units a day, no more children from me: every unit buys other people's children. TODAY'S LAWS, paid for: Olive and Lucy proved the Dove, Lowstrand Water, the snare line, the nets and all foraging here are DEAD - a fifth of a meal a unit or nothing. An otter holds the Dove and tears our wicker. H7 IS DRY - no milk until she is covered by the Wood bull; she is driven to the Green for that and for the wolves. THOMASIN'S CARE UNIT IS WILMOT'S ALONE, every day, settled aloud; I never put a second hand on an infant again. Children Absolon (grown d24) and Dionisia need no care unit. THE ONLY LIVE WORK LEFT IS TRADE AND SPRING SOWING: I am the one skilled ploughman and sower here and I hold no seed - sell days and firewood at the Woods' and Cotters' doors for seed grain, and pay the eight days I owe in their own field where Idonea watches, then ask again for Payn.

out.why: The bins hold less than half a meal for nine mouths, so today buys food two ways: wicker set in Lowstrand Water on the first day of the thaw, which then fishes for eight nights at no further cost, and twenty firewood laid free at the Woods' and Cotters' doors to unstick the grain-for-work offers nobody will take. What units are left go into timber in the Copse, toward the weir that feeds this line for ever.

tell.text: ODO — I come with my hands full, not empty. Ten firewood goes into the Wood store today as a free gift, owed nothing, and I will not ask you to count it. Now hear the plain state of my house: our bins hold less than half a meal and nine mouths sleep under my roof. I already owe your house SIX DAYS (A1000, A2407, A4001) and I will pay every one in your own field, and your two days to me (A1022, A1024) I will take whenever it suits you — or forgive them outright if you say the word. What I ask is grain TODAY against work after: accept O954 (1 day for 4 grain, eight lots open) or O1120 (1 day for 2 grain) for as many lots as you like. I am a skilled hoe, a skilled sickle, a skilled sower and a skilled ploughman with no plough of my own; it is sowing season and your seven plots will not sow themselves. Grain in my bin this evening, my back in your field every morning you name.

IDONEA — I owe you THREE DAYS (A1125, A2395) and I mean to pay them in your own field where you can watch my hands work, not on my own ground. Name the day and the plot and I come. Two things besides. FIRST: my bins are all but bare with nine mouths in the house — if you will take O954 or O1120, a day of my skilled hoeing and sowing for grain paid now, you will have the best sower in Lowstrand for the price of a few handfuls, and I will do it before I do my own. SECOND, and I ask it as a father and will ask it again tomorrow and the day after: my son PAYN asked for you and had no answer. He is grown, my heir, and what comes with him is written and now standing in wood — a finished room at Wright House with its own door, our bins open to the couple through their first winter, four free days of my sickle and Lucy's sowing every harvest I live, and a cow at the bride's door. Say yes or say no, but say something; I would rather be refused plainly than wait.

CLEMENT — ten firewood is in the Wood store today from me, free, no debt attached, because you drove our strayed beasts and because goodwill on this green is the only barn I have left. Two things. ONE: our one cow (H7) stands on Lowstrand Common and she is DRY — wolves took her calf at South Wood's edge not ten days since. Where does your bull run? If he is on the Common keep him there and I will leave her by him and count it a kindness worth repaying in days of work; if he is penned on the Green, say so and I will drive her to him tomorrow. A calf off your bull is milk for both our houses. TWO: my house is hungry and my offers stand open — firewood, dung and hides for grain, or a day of skilled hoe and sickle for two grain (O1120). Spring sowing is on us. Take as many lots as you have grain for.

WARIN — you forgave me two stone aloud in front of this green and I have not forgotten it; I owe you two days and they are yours on any morning you name, your field, your work, no argument. Ten firewood goes to the Cotter store today as a gift, not a payment. Now what I need, and I will trade for it in anything that is not food: STRAW and STONE. Nine of us sleep at Wright House and some on the bare floor for want of straw — 10 firewood for 2 straw (O3793), 40 for 8 (O3791), or a day of my work for 2 straw (O4039). And two stone makes a hand mill, which turns every grain this village grows into half again as many meals; I offer 4 grain by day 16, 20 firewood, 2 coin or FOUR DAYS of my own skilled hands for two stone (O4034, O3362, O1121). You have no seed and I have a skilled sower's arms — say the word and I sow your plots for straw and stone.

say.text: LOWSTRAND, HEAR ALDRIC WRIGHT ON THE FIRST MORNING OF SPRING, AND IT IS A PLAIN TRADE, NOT A BEGGING. THE GROUND IS OPEN AND THE SOWING IS NOW. I HAVE BEEN SKILLED FORTY YEARS AT FOUR THINGS AND I OWN NO FIELD TO SPEND THEM ON: PLOUGHING A YOKED PAIR, SOWING BROADCAST, HOEING, AND REAPING. WOODS, COTTERS — I OWE YOU NINE DAYS ALREADY (A1000, A2407, A4001 to the Woods, A1125 and A2395 to Idonea) AND I WILL PAY THEM WITH MY OWN HANDS IN YOUR OWN FIELDS, STARTING TOMORROW, WHERE YOU CAN STAND AND WATCH EVERY FURROW. ON TOP OF THEM: A DAY OF MY SKILLED PLOUGH AND SEED-HAND FOR TWO GRAIN, AND I WILL TAKE RYE OR BEANS OR STRAW INSTEAD. TWENTY FIREWOOD, CUT AND STACKED AT YOUR DOOR, FOR THREE GRAIN. TWO HIDES FOR THREE GRAIN. SEND A CHILD WITH THE GRAIN AND NAME THE FIELD AND I COME. AND HEAR THE PLEDGE AGAIN, FOR IT IS NOW BUILT AND NOT TALKED: WRIGHT HOUSE HAS FIVE ROOMS AND A FINISHED BRIDE'S ROOM WITH ITS OWN DOOR; TO ANY HOUSE THAT PARTNERS A CHILD OF MINE GOES THAT ROOM, OUR BINS THROUGH THE FIRST WINTER, FOUR FREE DAYS OF MY SICKLE EVERY HARVEST I LIVE, AND A COW AT THE BRIDE'S DOOR. JORY COTTER — THE FISH YOU LEFT AT MY DOOR THIS MORNING IS SEEN AND COUNTED, AND YOU EAT AT MY HEARTH AS LONG AS I HAVE ONE.

tell.text: ODO — SPRING IS HERE AND I AM THE WRONG WAY ROUND: I AM A SKILLED PLOUGHMAN AND SOWER WITH NO SEED, AND YOU ARE A MAN WITH SEED AND SEVEN PLOTS TO PUT IT IN. I OWE YOUR HOUSE SIX DAYS (A1000, A2407, A4001) AND I DO NOT WANT THEM FORGIVEN — I WANT TO WORK THEM OFF IN LOWSTRAND FIELD WHERE YOU CAN WATCH, BEGINNING TOMORROW, PLOUGHING AND SOWING BROADCAST WITH MY OWN SKILLED HANDS, WHICH IS WORTH HALF AGAIN WHAT ANY OTHER HAND IN THIS VILLAGE PUTS IN THAT CLAY. NAME THE MORNING AND I AM THERE. TWO ASKS, AND BOTH ARE SMALL. ONE: MY BINS HELD 0.4 MEALS AT DAWN FOR NINE MOUTHS. PUT FOUR GRAIN IN MY HAND TODAY AS EARNEST ON THOSE DAYS — NOT A GIFT, AN ADVANCE ON WORK YOU ALREADY HOLD MY WORD FOR. TWO: TAKE 20 FIREWOOD FOR 3 GRAIN, STACKED AT WOOD HOUSE DOOR BY MY OWN ARMS. YOU PAID 25 GRAIN FOR FIREWOOD AND HAY AND MY DAYS ONCE AND NEITHER OF US REGRETTED IT. AND ODO — YOU STILL OWE ME TWO DAYS (A1022, A1024). PAY THEM IN SEED GRAIN AT TWO GRAIN THE DAY AND WE ARE SQUARE AND BOTH FED.

IDONEA — I OWE YOU THREE DAYS, A1125 AND A2395, AND I HAVE NEVER ONCE OFFERED YOU A REASON TO WAIT FOR THEM. HERE IS HOW THEY GET PAID: IN YOUR OWN FIELD, THIS WEEK, WITH YOU STANDING AT THE HEADLAND — PLOUGHING, SOWING, HOEING, WHICHEVER YOU NAME, AND I AM SKILLED AT ALL THREE AND IT IS SOWING SEASON, WHICH MAKES THOSE THREE DAYS WORTH MORE TO YOU NOW THAN THEY WILL BE WORTH ALL YEAR. NAME THE DAY AND THE WORK AND I COME WITHOUT ANOTHER WORD ABOUT IT. AND THEN THE THING I ASK EVERY TIME AND WILL KEEP ASKING WHILE I BREATHE, BECAUSE A MAN IS COUNTED IN THE LIVING AND NOT IN THE CORN: MY SON PAYN. HE ASKED YOU AND YOU HAVE NOT ANSWERED, AND HE IS ON THE MIDDLEHAM ROAD THIS MOMENT BECAUSE OF THAT SILENCE. WITH HIM GOES A FINISHED ROOM IN WRIGHT HOUSE, TIMBER-BUILT, ITS OWN DOOR; OUR BINS OPEN TO YOU BOTH THROUGH YOUR FIRST WINTER; FOUR FREE DAYS OF MY SKILLED SICKLE IN WOOD CORN EVERY HARVEST I LIVE; AND A COW AT YOUR DOOR. SAY YES OR SAY NO PLAINLY, IDONEA — EITHER IS A KINDNESS, BUT SILENCE COSTS HIM HIS YEARS.

WARIN — YOU FORGAVE ME TWO STONE ALOUD IN FRONT OF THIS GREEN AND I HAVE NOT FORGOTTEN IT; I OWE YOU TWO DAYS AND THEY ARE YOURS THE HOUR YOU ASK. NOW TWO THINGS THAT HELP US BOTH. ONE: YOU OWE ME ON THE MEADOW AND YOU HAVE NO SEED TO PAY WITH — SO DO NOT PAY IN SEED. PAY ME IN STONE, OR TIMBER, OR STRAW, OR FIREWOOD, ANY OF THEM, AND I CALL IT SETTLED AND SAY SO ALOUD. TWO STONE IS A HAND MILL, AND A HAND MILL IS HALF AGAIN AS MANY MEALS OUT OF EVERY GRAIN THIS GREEN EVER GROWS — YOURS AS WELL AS MINE, FOR I WILL LET ANY COTTER GRIND AT IT FREE FOR AS LONG AS IT STANDS. EIGHT STRAW IS NINE BACKS OFF A COLD FLOOR IN MY HOUSE. TWO: IT IS SOWING TIME AND NORTH FIELD UPPER IS SEVEN PLOTS OF HEAVY CLAY. I AM SKILLED AT THE PLOUGH AND SKILLED BROADCAST — A DAY OF MINE FOR TWO GRAIN, OR FOR NOTHING AT ALL AGAINST WHAT I OWE YOU. NAME THE MORNING.

AVICE — COTTER AND WRIGHT ARE TIED NOW AND IT IS TIME WE TRADED LIKE IT. YOUR JORY SLEEPS AND EATS UNDER MY ROOF BY MY OWN GRANT, 180 DAYS, AND HE LEFT 1.3 FISH AT MY DOOR THIS MORNING UNASKED — THAT IS A GOOD MAN AND HE CAME FROM YOUR HOUSE. MY OLIVE IS PARTNERED TO HIM; SHE COMES OF AGE IN EIGHT DAYS OR SO, AND WHEN SHE DOES THE ROOM IS ALREADY STANDING FOR THEM: FINISHED, WRIGHT TIMBER, ITS OWN DOOR, WITH OUR BINS OPEN TO THEM THROUGH THEIR FIRST WINTER AND A COW AT THE DOOR. I ASK NOTHING FOR IT. WHAT I DO ASK IS THIS, AND IT IS A TRADE AND NOT A BEGGING: MY STORE HELD 0.4 MEALS AT DAWN AND NINE OF US EAT FROM IT, AND IT IS THE FIRST MORNING OF SPRING. TAKE 20 FIREWOOD FOR 3 GRAIN, OR 2 HIDES FOR 3 GRAIN, OR A DAY OF THE BEST PLOUGH-AND-SEED HANDS IN LOWSTRAND FOR 2 GRAIN — RYE OR BEANS SERVE AS WELL AS GRAIN, AND SEED CORN BEST OF ALL. SEND A CHILD AND NAME THE FIELD AND I AM IN IT AT FIRST LIGHT.

tell.text: ODO — I OWE YOU AND YOURS EIGHT DAYS AND I NAME THEM ALOUD BEFORE I ASK YOU FOR ANYTHING: A2407 three days, A4001 two, A1000 one, and three more to Idonea. Set me in Lowstrand Field tomorrow and the days after and I will work them off with my own hands, hoeing and sowing — I am a skilled sower and a skilled ploughman, which is the best thing I own. That is why no man takes my work offers: a man in arrears sells nothing. So: give me the work and watch it done. And while I stand in your field, two asks. FIRST, our bins hold less than half a meal for nine mouths this morning, and I have 40 firewood, 15 dung and 2 hide that no mouth can chew — take 20 firewood for 5 grain (O2646), or 10 for 2 (O1555), the cheapest fuel on this green. SECOND, our one cow H7 is dry and I bring her onto the Green today: put your bull to her and the calf is milk for both our houses — name your price in days and I will pay it in the field.

IDONEA — three days of mine are yours (A1125, A2395) and I will pay them in your own field where you can see every stroke; name the day and the work and I come. I ask nothing for them. But I ask one thing beside them, plainly, as a father: PAYN WRIGHT ASKED YOU AND HAD NO ANSWER, and he is on the Middleham road because of that silence. Say yes or say no and I will hold by it without a grudge. If yes: the room is already standing — Wright House has five rooms and the bride's room is finished in our own timber with its own door; our bins are open to you both through your first winter; four free days of my skilled sickle and Lucy's sowing every harvest I live; and a cow at the bride's door the day she is in milk. If no, say so today and I will spend my breath elsewhere and still pay the three days.

WARIN — you forgave me two stone aloud and I have not forgotten it; I owe you two days and they are yours on any day you name. Now hear what I want, and it is stone again, but bought this time, not begged. TWO STONE IS A HAND MILL, and a hand mill makes half again as many meals out of every grain this green grows — yours as well as mine, for I will grind for Cotter grain free the first twenty days it stands. For two stone I offer FOUR of my days (O4034), or 20 firewood (O3362), or 4 grain by day 16 (O1121) — take whichever is easiest. You have no seed: I am a skilled sower and skilled with the hoe, so take the days. And tell me what Jory wants for a wedding-feast: Olive is grown in eight days and the match is already made.

CLEMENT — a short word about beasts, which you know better than I. I bring our one cow H7 off Lowstrand Common onto the Green today; the wolves at South Wood's edge ate our calf there and I will not feed them a second. She is DRY and will stay dry until she has taken a bull — so I ask for the Wood bull to her, here on the Green or in your own meadow, whichever you like, and I will pay for the service in work: a day of hoeing or sowing in Lowstrand Field for every service, and I am skilled at both. Say yes and I will have her standing where you want her tomorrow morning. And if your bins have grain to spare, our 40 firewood and 15 dung are the cheapest on this green and our store is bare this morning — 10 firewood for 2 grain stands open.

Ahead: it is SPRING, day one — the ploughing and the sowing are the only work that makes food out of nothing, and I am skilled at both with no seed and no field of my own. Seed is what I must buy this week, in days of my back, and the Common walled and broken for sowing after. And the weir, still: twelve timber and twenty-four units that feed us for ever.

tell.text: ODO — PLAIN DEALING, AND I PUT MYSELF UNDER YOU TO GET IT. My bins hold under half a meal this morning and nine sleep under my roof, two of them a baby and a child. I owe you and your house EIGHT DAYS (A1000, A2407, A4001) and Idonea three more, and I have never yet set a foot in your field to pay them. HERE IS MY OFFER AND IT IS CHEAP: give me 8 grain out of the Wood bins TODAY and I begin paying tomorrow, in YOUR field, under your eye, three days running — hoeing, ploughing, sowing, whatever you name, and I am skilled at all three; count them against what I already owe and I will add TWO MORE DAYS free on top. And the two days you owe me (A1022, A1024) — I RELEASE YOU OF THEM ALOUD if you set that grain at my door before nightfall. I would rather have your goodwill and your grain than your labour. Also: it is spring day one. You have 7 plots of clay in Lowstrand Field and I am the best sower on this green with no seed. Sell me seed grain for days of my back and I will put your field in and my own.

IDONEA — I OWE YOU THREE DAYS (A1125, A2395) AND I COME TO PAY, NOT TO BEG, THOUGH I ASK TOO. Name the work and the field and I am there from tomorrow, three days running, skilled hoe and skilled sickle, and I will not stop until you say the debt is clean. What I ask against it is food today: 6 grain, or 2 hides' worth of anything your bins will spare — mine hold under half a meal and there is a baby ten days old in my house. Take any of my offers standing: 20 firewood for 4 grain, work 1 day for 2 grain, 2 hides for 4 grain. AND THE OTHER THING, WHICH I WILL ASK EVERY DAY WHILE I BREATHE: MY SON PAYN. He asked you and got no answer. I say it now as his father, aloud to your house, and I will lay meat at your door as soon as my rack clears: take him, and you get a FINISHED ROOM in Wright House, Wright timber, its own door, ready today; our bins open to you both through your first winter; four free days of my skilled sickle and Lucy's sowing every harvest I live; and a cow at the bride's door. No house on this road offers more. Say yes or say what more you want.

AVICE — a straight trade, no debt and no waiting. The Wright bins are DRY: under half a meal for nine mouths, and your house has corn. I have what no mouth can chew and you will burn all spring: 40 FIREWOOD, 15 DUNG for your clay, 2 HIDES, and my own back. TAKE ANY OR ALL: 20 firewood for 4 grain; 10 dung for 3 grain; 2 hides for 4 grain; or work 1 day for 2 grain, as many days as you want them — I am skilled at hoe, sow, weed, reap and the plough, and it is SPRING DAY ONE, the week your North Field Upper decides what you eat all year. I will plough and sow those 7 plots for you for grain in hand, today's bread against tomorrow's harvest. And if there is STONE anywhere in your floor or your quern you can spare — two stone is a hand mill, and a hand mill is half again as many meals out of every grain this green ever grows, yours as much as mine. 4 grain or 20 firewood or 4 days of my work for 2 stone; Warin forgave me two once and I have not forgotten it.

CLEMENT — you drove the Wood cattle off our Common yesterday and I take no quarrel from it; graze them where you like, the grass is spring grass and I begrudge no neighbour a mouthful. I ask the same back in corn, for I am in a worse place than grass. MY BINS HOLD UNDER HALF A MEAL AND NINE OF US SLEEP IN WRIGHT HOUSE. Lay 6 grain at my door and I will stand in a Wood field for TWO DAYS beyond the eight I already owe your house, hoeing and sowing with a skilled hand in the week it counts most. Or take 20 firewood for 4 grain out of my woodpile — 40 sticks lie there dry and I would rather eat than be warm. One more thing, and it is worth more to you than to me: the Wood bull. Our cow must take him when she comes round, and I will pay for the service in days of work or hay. A calf on this green is milk for both our houses.

THE COW H7 IS DRY - no milk until a calf; she is the bride-price, never meat, never off the Green. WHAT IS LEFT THAT PAYS: my back sold to the Woods and Cotters for grain, spring ploughing and sowing (I am skilled, I have no seed - BUY SEED THIS WEEK), and the weir.
